demonstration.narration: Now I'll turn the same pill around, so it keeps only that reason.
demonstration.reasoning: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning this one around swaps the everyday rejections for the increase itself, with no new filter to build.
demonstration.evidence: The pill reads ${param.incident.reason} again, without NOT, so only those rejections remain, and the hit count shows how many. Opening one will show which client they come from.

isolate.title: Turn the filter around to keep only that reason
isolate.narration: Now keep only the reason that increased. Click the NOT pill and choose Include results. The same filter then keeps that reason instead of leaving it out.
hints: Keep only the reason that increased, using the filter you already have.
Click the NOT pill to open its menu and choose Include results. (Deleting it and clicking the + next to the reason in its Top values works too.)
Turn the ${param.incident.reason} pill to Include results; Show me can do it for you.
isolate.concept: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning one around shows the other side of the same filter.
isolate.reasoning: One pill switches between the everyday rejections and the increase, so you compare the two views fairly.
isolate.evidence: Once the pill includes the reason, the hit count shows only those rejections.

demonstration.narration: I'll open one unusual rejection to see its reason and affected client in the same request.
demonstration.reasoning: A total can look convincing even when it includes other records. Opening one typical event shows the key values together, which a count alone can't do.
demonstration.evidence: This one rejection has ${param.incident.reason} and the ${param.incident.client} client together. So the unusual reason and the affected client really go together.

goal.title: Look at the rejection reasons in the window
goal.concept: A field's Top values show how often each value occurs. A reason that increased stands out from the everyday ones, without guessing.
goal.narration: Everyday rejections are mixed in with the increase. Open the authentication.rejection_reason field in the sidebar and read its Top values. Which reason makes up most of the window?
goal.reasoning: Leaving out reasons we think are normal would be a guess. Top values show how often each reason really occurs.
goal.evidence: The field's Top values show one reason far ahead of the routine ones: the most likely cause, and the one to check first.

demonstration.narration: Everyday rejections are mixed in with the increase. I'll check the rejection reason's Top values to see which reason makes up most of this window.
demonstration.reasoning: Leaving out reasons we think are normal would be a guess. Top values show how often each reason really occurs, so the filter comes from the data.
demonstration.evidence: The highlighted row, ${param.incident.reason}, makes up most of the rejections in the window, far ahead of the everyday reasons. That makes it the most likely cause of the increase, so we'll check it first. The next step leaves it out, to see whether the increase goes with it.

hints: Let the data show which rejection reason is the likeliest cause, instead of assuming which ones are normal.

goal.title: See the window without that reason
goal.concept: Filtering a value out shows everything else in the window. That is the normal background that an increase stands out from.
goal.narration: Some rejections happen every day. First, look at the window without the reason that stood out. In authentication.rejection_reason's Top values, click the − next to it to filter it out.
goal.reasoning: Leaving that reason out shows the everyday background on its own. Then you can see whether the increase goes with it, and how far it rises above the background.
goal.evidence: A NOT filter pill leaves that reason out, and the hit count and histogram fall to the everyday background.

demonstration.narration: First I'll filter out the most common reason, to see the window without it.
demonstration.reasoning: Some rejections happen every day. Leaving out the most common reason shows what's left on its own. If the increase goes with it, only the everyday background remains.
demonstration.evidence: The new filter pill, the small box under the query bar, reads NOT ${param.incident.reason}, so those rejections are left out. The hit count and histogram fall to the everyday background: normal traffic with a few ${param.incident.noise_reason_a} or ${param.incident.noise_reason_b} rejections. So the increase did go with ${param.incident.reason}.

hints: Look at the window without the reason that stood out, rather than at that reason alone.

Open authentication.rejection_reason's Top values and click the − next to the reason that stood out. That adds a NOT filter pill, a small box under the query bar that leaves the reason out. (Add filter with the operator ‘is not’ works too.)
Filter ${param.incident.reason} out with the − next to it in the Top values; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: That keeps only ${param.incident.reason}. This step looks at everything else first. Filter it out with the − instead; the next step turns the pill around.
You filtered on ${action.value}, one of the everyday reasons. This step leaves out the one that stood out in the Top values.

goal.title: Check that no other client has this rejection
goal.concept: A boolean query joins conditions with and, or and not. Asking for what shouldn't exist turns an empty result into evidence.
goal.narration: Now test whether any other client has this rejection. Search for the unusual reason and exclude the client in the event you opened. No results are expected: no other client had it.
goal.reasoning: One event shows the reason and the client together, but not that every such rejection comes from that client. A query for the reason from any other client tests exactly that.
goal.evidence: The query finds nothing, so the reason occurs only with that client.

demonstration.narration: I expect zero results here. I'll search for this rejection reason from any client except the one in the event we opened.
demonstration.reasoning: The event we opened pairs the reason with one client. But one event can't show that the reason never comes from anywhere else. A boolean query asks exactly that: this reason, and not this client. If nothing matches, the increase comes only from that client.
demonstration.evidence: An empty result is expected: no ${param.incident.reason} rejection in this window came from any client other than ${param.incident.client}. The empty search confirms the increase came only from that client. ${truth.conclusion}

hints: Show that the reason never comes from another client, rather than relying on the one event you opened.

In the query bar, join two conditions. The first is the rejection reason with its value. The second is not the client you found. Put a value with a hyphen in quotes. Here, no results is the answer you want.
Type authentication.rejection_reason: ${param.incident.reason} and not client.application.name: "${param.incident.client}"; Show me can do it for you.

drifts.note: That search found records, so it still includes the client you found. Ask for the reason from every client except that one, with not before the client condition.
